[ FILE 01 / 01 ] · EYES ONLY
// SUBJECT: THE OPERATIVE · 10 DIRECTIONS · 2026-08-10

Pick your
bloke.

Ten treatments across two batches. The first five are the same character rendered five ways — faithful to the ChatGPT mockup, varying only in how far each pushes from drawing toward mark. The second five are five different ideas about who he is. The interesting ones are in the second batch.

// SOURCE MATERIAL

What we fed it

Cut from the hero of redacted_digital_landingpage_preview_GPT2.png, with the surrounding copy, orange band and paper folder painted out so none of it bled into the generation.

Worth remembering the flaw you spotted in that mockup: it contained three different drawings of the same bloke at different angles and line weights, which is exactly why it read cheaper the longer you looked. The point of all this is landing on one canonical character we then reduce properly — full for hero, mid for nav, minimal for favicon and seal.

// BATCH ONE · SAME BLOKE, FIVE RENDERINGS

Variations on a theme

Most faithful to the original first, furthest pushed last.

[ 01 ]

Faithful

The reference character redrawn properly. Same angular construction, consistent line weights, no reinterpretation.

Works
Closest to the bloke you already responded to. The angular language is intact and the tie reads.
Doesn't
Compositionally the loosest. The figure leans right, the coat fragments into floating slivers, dead space bottom-right. A drawing, not a mark.
Verdict
Safe and unsurprising. Would need tightening before it could be a logo.
[ 02 ]

Bold Logo

Simplified aggressively into a mark. Fewer shapes, heavier masses, built to survive at 8mm.

Works
Closes into a single enclosed silhouette, so it reads as one object rather than a pile of shards. Best small-size survival in batch one.
Doesn't
Drifted more front-facing than the three-quarter we asked for, and there is a faint hint of facial features where we wanted pure shadow.
Verdict
The best pure mark of batch one — but batch two beat it at its own job.
[ 03 ]

Stencil

Cut as a hard military spray-stencil with bridge gaps, as if sprayed through a card template.

Works
Distinctive and on-theme. Nobody in the local market looks like this. The sprayed edge sells the ops fiction.
Doesn't
Soft sprayed edges will not vectorise cleanly and are exactly what dies small and in print. Fights the crisp grid language of the site.
Verdict
Beautiful and awkward. A texture, not a mark.
[ 04 ]

Noir Print

1950s film-noir screenprint. Flat two-tone with hard-edged chiaroscuro across brim and coat.

Works
The most dramatic of batch one, and the best as a large hero illustration. Cream masses are solid rather than splintered.
Doesn't
Still too detailed to reduce. A poster, not a logo.
Verdict
Strong hero candidate, no use small.
[ 05 ]

Silhouette

Reduced to an almost pure silhouette. Meant for favicon, wax seal and single-colour deboss.

Works
Restrained and calm. Elegant large.
Doesn't
Misses its own brief. Reduction was read as thinner, so it came out as hairlines — precisely what vanishes at 24px and clogs in print.
Verdict
An instructive failure. Worth seeing, not worth building on.
// BATCH TWO · FIVE DIFFERENT IDEAS

Actually different

Same palette, same rules, same faceless-under-the-brim discipline — but five different answers to the question of who he is and what job he does. This is where the deck gets interesting.

[ 06 ]

The Tradie Operative

A spy who works for tradespeople. Hi-vis vest with reflective banding under the trench coat.

Works
This is the actual brand idea made visible — the collision of intelligence agency and worksite that the whole business is built on. It lands the joke in one image, without a word of copy. It also came back inverted on cream, which accidentally answers the paper-surface question below.
Doesn't
The most niche. It commits hard to the gag, and a gag is harder to live with for five years than a straight character. Also the least useful small — the vest detail is the whole point and it is the first thing to disappear.
Verdict
The boldest strategic swing here. Either your favourite thing in the deck or too much — no middle ground.
[ 07 ]

Full Figure

Whole standing figure, coat in motion, dossier folder in hand. Cinematic hero anchor rather than a badge.

Works
The only one that could genuinely anchor the left side of a hero at full height. Motion and the orange folder give it narrative that a bust cannot.
Doesn't
Defective. Look closely — there are two overlapping hats and a doubled figure. A generation artefact, not a design choice. The concept is sound; this particular render is not usable.
Verdict
Worth re-running rather than judging. The idea deserves a clean attempt.
[ 08 ]

Redaction-Native

The character's identity is literally redacted — a hard black censor bar struck across the eye-line as an integral part of the design.

Works
The strongest idea across both batches. The company is called Redacted Digital and the mascot is redacted. It fuses the mascot with the single most distinctive device in the brand, so the character and the name explain each other. Bold, memorable, and it stays legible small because the bar is a solid mass.
Doesn't
Ties you to the bar forever. If the redaction motif ever gets tired, the mascot goes with it.
Verdict
My pick for the character. Nothing else in the deck is this ownable.
[ 09 ]

Agency Seal

A circular department emblem. Silhouetted operative bust, concentric tick-mark ring, star at the base.

Works
Purpose-built for the jobs a character portrait is bad at — favicon, wax seal, business-card deboss, stamp on a proposal. Symmetrical, institutional, crisp. It is the only one of the ten that is finished for its intended use rather than needing reduction work.
Doesn't
Not a character. It cannot carry a hero on its own and it has no personality to speak of.
Verdict
My pick for the mark. Pair it with 08 and the pair covers everything.
[ 10 ]

Surveillance

The operative as evidence — coarse halftone, torn paper edge, caught unaware rather than posed.

Works
The most atmospheric. The torn edge and halftone read as an artefact pulled from a file rather than a logo, which is a genuinely different register to everything else.
Doesn't
The figure is hard to read. Halftone dots and a torn edge are the two things that reproduce worst at small sizes and in print.
Verdict
A texture or a section device. Not the mascot.
// SCALE TEST

The test that actually decides it

Everything looks good at 700px. What matters is nav size, favicon size, and roughly the size it prints on a business card. Squint at the last two columns — the answer there is not the one the big versions suggest.

// RECOMMENDATION

Where I'd land

Archie's pick

08 is the character. 09 is the mark.

08 Redaction-Native is the best idea in either batch, and it is not close. The company is called Redacted Digital and the mascot has a censor bar struck across his eyes. The character and the name explain each other, which is the thing a mascot is supposed to do and almost never does. It is also bold enough to survive small, because the bar is a solid mass rather than fine linework.

09 Agency Seal is the only asset in the deck that is finished for its job. Favicon, wax seal, card deboss, stamp on a proposal — it does all of them today, with no reduction work needed. A character portrait is bad at exactly those jobs.

Together they cover the whole system: 08 carries the hero and anywhere the brand needs personality, 09 carries every small and official use. Same world, different jobs, no compromise in either.

The wildcard is 06. The hi-vis under the trench coat is the actual business idea in one image — an intelligence agency for blokes on the tools. It is either the best thing here or too much, and that is genuinely your call, not mine.

Flag

Nine of the ten assume a dark background

They are cream linework on near-black, with the black doing double duty as background and as the interior of the hat and coat. You cannot simply knock the background out for a transparent PNG — you would be left with floating cream shards.

That matters because three of the seven homepage sections sit on warm paper. The winner needs a deliberate inverted treatment, not an automated cutout. 06 is the exception — it came back inverted on cream of its own accord, which is an accidental but genuinely useful preview of what the paper-surface version wants to look like.

Defect

07 is broken, not bad

Look closely at the full-figure variant and there are two overlapping hats and a doubled body. That is a generation artefact, not a design decision. The concept — a full standing figure with a dossier under one arm, anchoring the hero at full height — is the only one that could carry a hero without a bust crop. It deserves a clean re-run before you write it off.

  1. Pick a direction, or point at one and ask for five more around it. Iterating is cheap now and expensive after vectorising.
  2. Re-run 07 clean if the full-figure idea appeals — one generation, not a project.
  3. Redraw the winner as real vector. These are AI raster with slightly inconsistent edges; print and small sizes need actual paths, and that is a redraw rather than an auto-trace.
  4. Build the three detail levels — full for hero, mid for nav and cards, minimal for favicon and seal. Same angle throughout so it always reads as one bloke. If 09 wins the mark, the minimal level is already done.
  5. Solve the paper-surface treatment per the flag above.
  6. Then the business cards are unblocked — which is what started all of this.
